Where it began

Josh Inglis was born in Leeds, West Yorkshire, on 4 March 1995. When he was 14 his family moved to Australia, and that is where his cricket grew up. His first taste of first-class cricket came in December 2015, for a Cricket Australia XI against the touring West Indians. He settled in with Western Australia and, in the Big Bash League, Perth Scorchers.

The big scores followed. In October 2020, in the first round of the Sheffield Shield, he made his maiden first-class hundred, an unbeaten 153 against South Australia. The next English summer he joined Leicestershire for the T20 Blast and made two centuries there, the second an unbeaten 118 from 61 balls against Worcestershire.

The player

Inglis broke into the Australian side as a wicketkeeper-batter in white-ball cricket, making his T20 international debut against Sri Lanka in February 2022 and his one-day debut that June. He was in the squad that won the 2023 World Cup, and he made T20 international hundreds against India in November 2023 and against Scotland in September 2024, the second reaching three figures in 43 balls, the fastest by an Australian in that format at the time. He also captained Australia in both short formats, standing in for Pat Cummins in a one-day match against Pakistan in November 2024.

His Test chance came in Sri Lanka in January 2025. Geoff Marsh handed him his cap, making him the 470th man to play Tests for Australia, and he made a hundred on debut, becoming the fourth Australian with centuries in all three formats. He played once against West Indies that July and twice in the 2025–26 Ashes. By November 2026 he had played 6 Tests between 2025 and 2026, scoring 290 runs at 32.22 with 2 hundreds and a best of 102, and had held 2 catches.

What made him special

Inglis liked to get on with it. His short-format hundreds tended to arrive in a rush, and he was just as lively in the field: in the Brisbane Test of the 2025–26 Ashes he ran out England's captain, Ben Stokes, while falling away from the stumps.

His Test runs came in large helpings rather than small ones. By November 2026 he had two Test hundreds and not a single fifty, which suggests that once he was in, stopping halfway did not much appeal to him.

Away from the middle

His cricket took him well beyond Perth: to Leicestershire for an English summer and to Lucknow Super Giants in the IPL. Along the way he picked up a World Cup win, a turn as stand-in captain and a baggy green, which made for a busy few years.

And finally

Patience was part of his story. He was in the squad that won the 2021 T20 World Cup before he had played a T20 international, and in the squad that won the 2023 World Test Championship final well before his first Test, which came in January 2025. Few players have had so much practice at winning before they got a game.
